title: Adaptive thermal comfort and sustainable thermal standards for buildings

findings.antecedent: rational thermal comfort indices (e.g., ISO 7730, ASHRAE 55)
findings.consequent: prediction of comfort vote in field surveys
findings.mechanism: Rational indices fail to capture the adaptive processes observed in real-world field studies.
findings.quote: When rational indices are used to predict the thermal comfort of subjects measured in field surveys they are found to be no better at predicting the comfort vote [6] than simpler indices such as temperature alone.

findings.antecedent: conditions in field surveys
findings.consequent: range of conditions subjects find comfortable
findings.mechanism: Adaptive actions by occupants allow for a wider range of comfortable conditions than predicted by rational indices.
findings.quote: In addition the range of conditions which subjects find comfortable in field surveys is much wider than the rational indices predict.

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (comparison across surveys vs. within a single survey)
findings.consequent: rate of change of mean comfort vote
findings.mechanism: People adapt to different climates, making their comfort vote less sensitive to temperature changes when comparing across diverse contexts than within a single, more stable context.
findings.quote: The rate of change of comfort vote with temperature is characteristically much lower from one survey to another than it is within any particular survey (Fig. 1).

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (in field surveys over a wide range of indoor climates)
findings.mechanism: Occupants adapt their comfort expectations and behaviors to the prevailing indoor temperature.
findings.quote: The corollary of this finding is that in field surveys the comfort temperature is closely correlated with the mean temperature measured. This was found to be the case in surveys conducted over a wide range of indoor climates (Fig. 2a).

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (measured at monthly intervals throughout the year in Pakistan and Europe)
findings.mechanism: People continuously adapt their comfort expectations and behaviors to seasonal changes in indoor temperature.
findings.quote: The strong relationship with comfort temperature is clear.

findings.antecedent: indoor temperature (20-30 °C) with fans (in Pakistani offices)
findings.mechanism: Adaptive actions, such as using fans, allow occupants to maintain comfort over a wider range of indoor temperatures.
findings.quote: Pakistani buildings were found comfortable at temperatures ranging between 20 and 30 °C with no cooling apart from fans (from [12]).

findings.antecedent: outdoor monthly mean temperature (in free-running buildings)
findings.mechanism: In free-running buildings, the indoor climate is directly coupled to outdoor conditions, and occupants adapt their comfort expectations accordingly.
findings.quote: The relationship for the free-running buildings was closely linear.

findings.antecedent: outdoor monthly mean temperature (in heated or cooled buildings)
findings.mechanism: In heated or cooled buildings, the indoor climate is decoupled from the outdoor temperature, making the direct adaptive relationship less pronounced.
findings.quote: For heated and cooled buildings the relationship is more complex.

findings.antecedent: building type distinction (centrally air-conditioned vs. naturally ventilated) for predicting occupant thermal response
findings.mechanism: The distinction based on building services (AC vs. NV) is not supported by field evidence as a primary driver of adaptive response, suggesting more fundamental adaptive mechanisms.
findings.quote: Nor is this distinction supported by evidence from the field [6].

findings.antecedent: building type distinction (free-running vs. heated or cooled buildings)
findings.consequent: precision of the relationship between comfort temperature and outdoor temperature
findings.mechanism: This distinction better captures the degree of environmental control and adaptive opportunity, leading to more precise relationships.
findings.quote: Humphreys and Nicol [14] argue that using Humphreys' original distinction (between free-running and heated or cooled buildings) increases the precision of the relationship...

findings.antecedent: occupant access to building controls
findings.mechanism: Control over one's environment provides affordances for adaptation, leading to higher satisfaction and tolerance for minor discomforts.
findings.quote: Leaman and Bordass [20] have demonstrated that there is more 'forgiveness' of buildings in which occupants have more access to building controls.

findings.antecedent: occupant control over conditions (e.g., opening windows, using fans)
findings.mechanism: When occupants can adjust their environment, variability can be a positive outcome of their adaptive actions to maintain comfort.
findings.quote: In buildings where the occupants are in control, variability may result from people adjusting conditions to suit themselves. A certain amount of variability then becomes a 'good thing'.

findings.antecedent: control left to building manager (through HVAC system)
findings.mechanism: Lack of personal control limits adaptive opportunities, making occupants less forgiving and reducing the range of acceptable conditions.
findings.quote: If the control is left to the building manager (through the HVAC system) there is a smaller envelope of acceptable conditions, comfort changes more quickly with temperature and the occupants appear less forgiving.

findings.antecedent: alpha value for exponentially-weighted running mean outdoor temperature (Trm)
findings.consequent: correlation of Trm with comfort temperature
findings.mechanism: The exponentially-weighted running mean with an alpha value of approximately 0.8 best reflects the temporal dynamics of human adaptation to past temperatures.
findings.quote: The correlation with Tod falls consistently with increasing a, the correlation with comfort temperature rises gradually until a reaches about 0.8 and then starts to decrease.

findings.antecedent: daily mean outdoor temperature (alpha=0) and monthly mean outdoor temperature (alpha≈0.95)
findings.mechanism: Neither instantaneous daily mean nor long-term monthly mean temperatures fully capture the temporal aspect of adaptation as effectively as an exponentially-weighted running mean.
findings.quote: The correlation with Tod (x = 0) and with the monthly mean of outdoor temperature (α≈ 0.95) are both less than the correlation with Trm where a = 0.8.

findings.antecedent: control regime with variable indoor set-point (changing with running mean outdoor temperature) compared to constant set-point
findings.mechanism: People's adaptive capacity allows them to remain comfortable even with a variable indoor temperature set-point, as long as it aligns with the running mean of outdoor temperature.
findings.quote: Recent work suggests that the use of a control regime which provides a set-point temperature changing with the running mean of the outdoor temperature does not increase discomfort among occupants as compared with a constant set-point...

findings.antecedent: control regime with variable indoor set-point (changing with running mean outdoor temperature) compared to constant set-point
findings.mechanism: Aligning indoor temperature set-points with outdoor conditions through adaptive algorithms reduces the energy demand for cooling.
findings.quote: ...but can result in substantial savings in energy use [13].

findings.antecedent: free-running buildings (data from 1970s [9] and 1998 ASHRAE database [15])
findings.consequent: relationship between comfort temperature (Tc) and outdoor temperature (To) (Tc = 13.5 + 0.54 To)
findings.mechanism: The fundamental adaptive mechanisms linking outdoor climate to indoor comfort in free-running buildings are remarkably stable across different datasets and time periods.
findings.quote: Humphreys and Nicol [14] showed that this relationship between comfort temperature Tc and outdoor temperature To for free-running buildings (Eq. (2)) is remarkably stable as between data presented by Humphreys in the 1970s [9] and in the 1998 ASHRAE database [15] (see Fig. 5).

findings.antecedent: relationship Tc = 13.5 + 0.54 To (for free-running buildings)
findings.mechanism: This high correlation quantifies the strong adaptive relationship between outdoor temperature and comfort in free-running buildings.
findings.quote: The correlation coefficient r for the relationship was 0.97 for 1978 data and 0.95 for ASHRAE database.

findings.antecedent: heated and cooled buildings (comparison between 1970s [9] and 1990s [11] databases)
findings.mechanism: Changes in custom, expectations, or other factors over time may influence preferred comfort temperatures in controlled environments.
findings.quote: There is also a difference of some 2 °C in indoor comfort temperatures for heated and cooled buildings between two databases [9], one compiled in the late 1970s and the other [11] compiled in the 1990s (see Fig. 5).

findings.antecedent: no possibility of changing clothing, activity, or air movement
findings.mechanism: The absence of adaptive opportunities severely restricts the range of thermal conditions perceived as comfortable.
findings.quote: In a situation where there was no possibility of changing clothing or activity and where air movement cannot be used, the comfort zone may be as narrow as ± 2 °C.

findings.antecedent: adaptive opportunities available and appropriate (e.g., changing clothing, activity, using air movement)
findings.mechanism: The ability to perform adaptive actions allows individuals to maintain comfort over a significantly wider range of environmental conditions.
findings.quote: In situations where these adaptive opportunities are available and appropriate the comfort zone may be considerably wider.

findings.antecedent: use of a variable indoor temperature in air-conditioned buildings
findings.mechanism: Allowing indoor temperatures to vary adaptively with outdoor conditions reduces the energy required for cooling.
findings.quote: The extent of energy savings has been estimated in the region of 10% of the cooling load in UK conditions. In a recent European project [31] estimated energy savings were in the region of 18%.

findings.antecedent: naturally ventilated buildings
findings.mechanism: Naturally ventilated buildings rely on adaptive comfort, which inherently requires less energy for conditioning compared to air-conditioned buildings.
findings.quote: Naturally ventilated buildings typically use about half the energy of ones which are air-conditioned [32].

tables.description: Descriptors for the ASHRAE and Bedford scales for thermal sensation votes

limitations: Environmental conditions in field studies are inherently variable and difficult to measure accurately, leading to potential errors in statistical relationships.
It is difficult to generalize results from one field survey to another due to contextual differences.
Rational indices require knowledge of clothing insulation and metabolic rate, which are difficult to estimate accurately in the field.
Quantifying 'adaptive opportunity' in terms of building controls is difficult, as the mere existence of a control does not guarantee its use or effectiveness.
Comfort surveys do not consistently produce data coherent enough for a precise statistical determination of the best time-series to use for adaptive algorithms.
It is unclear whether observed differences in comfort temperatures for heated/cooled buildings over time are due to changes in preference or other database differences.
